promptText: What event is conventionally treated as the founding of Artificial Intelligence as a named discipline?
options: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'
The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
The 1943 McCulloch-Pitts artificial neuron paper
Rosenblatt's 1958 Perceptron demonstration
explanation: The 1956 Dartmouth Conference coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' and is conventionally treated as the field's founding, complete with the (badly overoptimistic) proposal that a small group could make major progress in one summer.

promptText: What mathematical result directly triggered the first AI winter for neural network research?
options: Minsky and Papert's 1969 proof that a single-layer perceptron cannot learn the XOR function
Turing's proof that machines can never think
Shannon's information theory results from the 1940s
Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's 1986 backpropagation paper
explanation: The 1969 book Perceptrons proved a structural limitation of single-layer networks and was widely (if incorrectly) over-generalized to multi-layer networks too, freezing funding for over a decade.

promptText: What algorithm, popularized in 1986, made training multi-layer neural networks practical?
options: Gradient boosting
Backpropagation
K-means clustering
Support vector machines
explanation: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's 1986 paper showed how the chain rule could be applied systematically layer by layer, directly refuting the earlier narrative that networks couldn't learn XOR-like patterns.

promptText: What made AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win historically significant, beyond just winning a competition?
options: It was the first system in history to use any labeled training data
It proved that learned representations from raw data could decisively beat decades of hand-engineered computer vision features
It was the first commercially deployed expert system
It eliminated the need for GPUs in future model training
explanation: AlexNet beat every prior hand-engineered computer vision pipeline by a stunning margin, convincing the field almost overnight that letting a model learn its own features from raw data at scale was the winning approach.

promptText: What was XCON (also known as R1) used for at Digital Equipment Corporation?
options: Diagnosing bacterial blood infections in patients
Automatically configuring VAX computer orders using a rule-based expert system
Training early neural networks on GPU hardware
Translating natural language between English and Japanese
explanation: XCON used thousands of interacting rules to configure computer orders correctly, reportedly saving DEC tens of millions of dollars a year and serving as an early proof that rule-based systems could deliver real commercial value.

promptText: What did the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' introduce?
options: The original Perceptron architecture
The backpropagation algorithm
The Transformer architecture
The concept of an AI winter
explanation: The Transformer replaced recurrent sequence processing with an attention mechanism computable in parallel across sequence positions, which is the direct ancestor of every model discussed in the rest of the series.

promptText: Why is Deep Blue's 1997 chess victory considered a fundamentally different achievement from AlphaGo's 2016 Go victory?
options: Deep Blue used deep neural networks while AlphaGo relied purely on brute-force search
Deep Blue relied largely on brute-force search over a hand-built evaluation function, whereas Go's much larger search space required genuine learned pattern recognition combined with search
AlphaGo ran significantly slower than Deep Blue on equivalent hardware
Deep Blue's chess victory required no computation at inference time
explanation: The chapter uses this contrast to show that 'beating humans at a narrow game' and 'general intelligence' are different achievements even between two narrow-game wins — one via search over rules, one via learned pattern recognition plus search.

promptText: What key correction did DeepMind's 'Chinchilla' paper make to earlier scaling-law practice?
options: It proved that larger models are always worse than smaller ones
It showed many earlier large models were undertrained relative to their size, and that for a fixed compute budget, model size and training data size need to scale together
It disproved the existence of scaling laws entirely
It showed that data quality has no measurable effect on model quality
explanation: Chinchilla corrected the assumption that model size alone drives quality — many pre-2022 models could have reached the same quality with fewer parameters and proportionally more training data.

promptText: MYCIN reportedly outperformed junior physicians in diagnostic trials, yet was never widely deployed clinically. Why, per the chapter?
options: It was too computationally slow to be usable in a hospital setting
Integration into clinical workflow, liability and accountability questions, and manual data-entry burdens blocked adoption — not its diagnostic accuracy
It was formally banned by medical regulators for ethical violations
It required internet connectivity that did not exist at the time
explanation: Performance on a narrow benchmark was not the blocker; nobody could answer who was liable if MYCIN was wrong, and it didn't fit real clinical workflow — an early precursor to today's human-in-the-loop and liability debates.

promptText: What is the key mechanical difference between forward-chaining and backward-chaining inference engines?
options: Forward chaining only works on numeric data, backward chaining only on text

Forward chaining derives new facts from known facts until no more can be derived (data-driven), while backward chaining starts from a hypothesis and works backward to check what evidence would support it (goal-driven)
The two techniques are functionally identical and differ only in name
Backward chaining does not use any rules at all, only statistics
explanation: MYCIN used backward chaining because it is more efficient when the space of possible conclusions (candidate diagnoses) is well understood in advance — it only checks the facts relevant to the hypothesis being tested.

promptText: Why did Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Project (1982-1992) fail to achieve its stated ambitions?
options: It ran out of government funding after only one year
It bet heavily on specialized logic-programming hardware right as the field's center of gravity was shifting toward statistical, data-driven methods that didn't need that hardware
It successfully achieved AGI but was shut down for ethical reasons
It was a purely theoretical research exercise with no engineering component at all
explanation: By the time the decade-long project concluded, commodity workstations outperformed its specialized machines, and the statistical ML approaches that mattered for the next twenty years didn't require the symbolic-inference hardware it had optimized for.

promptText: Why do modern AI guardrail and policy layers often resemble a 'return' to symbolic rule engines, per the chapter's argument?
options: It is genuinely ironic and inconsistent with why symbolic AI was originally abandoned

It is expected, not ironic — symbolic rules were abandoned as the primary mechanism for producing broad, general capability, not because determinism and auditability were bad properties, and guardrails need exactly that narrow, auditable profile
Guardrails are actually implemented internally as neural networks, not as rules at all
Rule-based engines were never actually abandoned by the field in the first place
explanation: Guardrails don't need open-ended knowledge; they need a small, well-scoped, auditable set of hard constraints, which is precisely the profile symbolic rules are good at — hence their resurfacing as a wrapper rather than the core reasoning mechanism.

promptText: XCON delivered real, measurable commercial value, yet the broader expert-systems industry still collapsed into a second AI winter. What best resolves this apparent contradiction?
options: XCON was secretly a failure and its success was fabricated for publicity

XCON's success was narrow and domain-bounded, but the industry wrongly generalized that the same hand-authored approach would scale to messier, less-bounded domains — the resulting gap between promise and delivered value across the industry triggered the funding collapse
The second AI winter was caused entirely by a hardware shortage unrelated to expert systems
DEC's later bankruptcy directly and solely caused the second AI winter
explanation: XCON worked because DEC's configuration domain had a well-bounded, stable rule structure; the mistake was assuming that success would generalize to open-ended domains like medical diagnosis at scale, where costs proved far higher than projected.

promptText: The chapter frames the knowledge acquisition bottleneck as a 'scaling mismatch.' What exactly is being mismatched?
options: GPU memory bandwidth versus CPU clock speed

The number of rules needed for real-world coverage grows combinatorially (each new rule can conflict with every existing one), while human authoring throughput only grows linearly with headcount — unlike a statistical model, where adding training examples doesn't require manually checking for logical conflicts with every prior example
The volume of labeled data versus the volume of unlabeled data available on the internet
The speed of backpropagation versus the speed of plain gradient descent
explanation: As a rule base grows, verifying that a new rule doesn't silently break an old one requires understanding the whole system, so maintenance cost grows faster than coverage — a scaling mismatch that has no analogue in statistical or learned systems.

promptText: The chapter argues 'the current era's success is partly a matter of enabling infrastructure lining up, not proof that connectionism was always the correct theory of intelligence.' Why is this an important caution for evaluating today's dominant AI paradigm?
options: It implies connectionism was always mathematically inferior to symbolic AI and only won by luck

It implies that the internet (data) and GPUs (compute) happening to arrive together resolved connectionism's historical weakness — a caution against assuming permanent dominance for a paradigm that won partly due to external, replaceable infrastructure factors rather than provable theoretical superiority
It proves that scaling laws are guaranteed to hold indefinitely into the future
It means expert systems are scheduled to make a commercial comeback next
explanation: The two camps' seventy-year argument was decided by which camp's weakness got solved first by outside forces, not by philosophy — a reminder that today's paradigm shift could itself be contingent on infrastructure rather than a settled, final answer.
